video_title: People Hate These 5 Stocks But They'll Be Wrong | TCAF 261
gist: On The Compound and Friends, Josh Brown and Michael Batnick host value investor Jonathan Boyar (Boyar Value Group), who argues that 2026's junk-over-quality rally, pod-shop risk limits and programmatic 'AI loser' basket selling (triggered by the Muse and Instinct AI agents) have compressed multiples on sound businesses. His 'fresh look' names include Booking, Airbnb, Broadridge, Pool Corp, Restaurant Brands (QSR), Comcast and MGM, alongside a still-intact Uber thesis. The hosts add color on McDonald's, Nike, Schwab, casinos and VICI Properties.

insights.claim: Adam Parker data show only 23.2% of the top 500 US stocks held for 10 years beat the S&P 500, and 27.7% over three-year holding periods, with the hit rate trending lower since 2002.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Stock pickers must accept heavy concentration in the few long-term winners, or index. The base rate is against most single-stock holdings.
insights.quote: only 23.2% of the top uh 500 US stocks held for 10 years beat the index

insights.claim: Michael Batnick notes the share of stocks beating the S&P 500 was falling well before Apple and the Mag 7 dominated, and says it would only recover toward 50% in something like an AI meltdown in which Apple, Nvidia, Google and Meta fall around 70%.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Market breadth is unlikely to improve without a mega-cap AI unwind, which is effectively the one scenario that would favor equal-weight and active stock picking.

insights.claim: Jonathan Boyar argues buy-and-hold is the result of an investment strategy, not a strategy in itself: you hold great companies bought at reasonable prices while continuously re-checking execution, competition and valuation.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Boyar
insights.so_what: Holding periods should follow from fundamentals and valuation checks, not from a fixed rule.
insights.quote: buy and hold is a result of an investment strategy, not an investment strategy in and of itself

insights.claim: Jonathan Boyar says Boyar Asset Management's mostly taxable accounts let winners run somewhat past fair value, because after capital-gains tax a replacement must be roughly 25% better to justify switching. He is comfortable with 10-15% positions such as Microsoft, which the S&P 500 already holds at about 6%.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Boyar
insights.so_what: In taxable portfolios the tax drag sets a high bar for trimming winners, so concentration drift is often rational.

insights.claim: Jonathan Boyar held Microsoft through a painful early-2026 drawdown from about $579 and says the stock is 'now back', arguing that trying to sell the top and rebuy the trough would have left his clients worse off.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Boyar
insights.so_what: Boyar treats sitting through drawdowns in high-quality compounders as the price of owning them, rather than trying to trade around them.

insights.claim: Jonathan Boyar cites Warren Buffett's own view that one of his biggest mistakes was not selling Coca-Cola at 60 times earnings in 1998, after which it badly lagged the S&P 500. Boyar's point is that a great business at a terrible valuation still produces poor returns.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Boyar
insights.so_what: This is a caution for today's premium-multiple quality names: the starting valuation can erase years of returns.
insights.quote: Great business, terrible valuation

insights.claim: Josh Brown argues the media wrongly presents trims as a loss of conviction, when trimming can simply reflect position size after a big run-up or a need for capital for other ideas. Boyar counters, citing Chris Mayer's 100-Baggers, that trimming winners like Apple has usually been wrong and triggers taxes.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Treat trimming as a sizing and tax decision, not a verdict on the business, and recognize that doing nothing often wins.
insights.quote: We don't talk about position sizing and trading around positions on TV almost because it's like a gotcha moment.

insights.claim: The hosts and Jonathan Boyar agree deep-value 'cigar butt' investing (net-nets, broken retailers) no longer works now that information is widely available, and Boyar describes himself as a value-oriented opportunist buying durable businesses below intrinsic value, closer to GARP.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Boyar
insights.so_what: Value exposure should favor quality compounders at reasonable prices over statistically cheap declining businesses.
insights.quote: Deep deep value is maybe the worst strategy on the planet.

insights.claim: Jonathan Boyar avoids catching falling knives, noting Pool Corp looked cheap at $400, $300 and $200, and instead starts falling stocks with about a 2% position so he can add later. The hosts add that a stock that stops falling on continued bad news signals sellers are exhausted.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Boyar
insights.so_what: Scale into broken stocks in stages, and use resilience to bad news as the entry confirmation.
insights.quote: maybe I'll buy a 2% position with the hope of adding more later on because no one's ever going to be able to pick a bottom

insights.claim: In 2026 one of the best strategies has been owning the junkiest stocks and shorting high-quality ones: a chart from Julian Klotchko shows the Goldman Sachs most-shorted basket up 40% year to date, while the long-quality/short-junk pair is down 23%.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Quality factor exposure has been a major drag this year. A reversal of junk leadership could be a sizable mean-reversion opportunity.
insights.quote: the Goldman Sachs most shorted basket is up 40% year-to date

insights.claim: McDonald's, a high-return-on-equity quality business, is down 29% over 144 days from a February 2026 peak, a crash the host says is rare for the stock, last seen around COVID and before that the dot-com bust.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Quality defensives are being sold like cyclicals, a potential contrarian entry point in QSR names.
insights.quote: It's down 29% over the last 144 days.

insights.claim: Jonathan Boyar has presented on a possible 'quality bubble' comparable to the Nifty Fifty, pointing to names like Cintas and Costco. The hosts note Walmart and Costco at roughly 40-50 times earnings, which Boyar says only works for 30-year holders.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Boyar
insights.so_what: Premium-multiple staples and quality compounders carry derating risk even if the businesses keep executing.
insights.quote: You know, it's hard to make a money if you buy a stock at 60 times earnings.

insights.claim: The hosts call Nike the poster child for how multiple derating hurts buy-and-hold investors: earnings have fallen for about five years while the premium multiple keeps compressing, so the stock has done worse than the fundamentals. They blame the direct-to-consumer push that alienated Foot Locker, Amazon and Dick's, reliance on the Jordan brand, stronger competitors, and athletes now going direct to consumers.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Boyar passes on Nike despite the drawdown. A falling multiple on top of falling earnings means a cheap-looking stock may still not be a buy.
insights.quote: you could have a stock get cut in half, still not be cheap

insights.claim: Multiple compression in 2026 has hit every sector except staples. Jonathan Boyar attributes it to several causes together: a roughly 5% 10-year yield (which he says investors will take a couple of years to adjust to, though stocks did fine with 5% yields in the 1990s), perceived AI disruption, and lingering COVID hangovers.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Boyar
insights.so_what: If rates are only part of the story, AI-fear derating on businesses that are not actually disrupted is where the mispricing lies.
insights.quote: it's going to take investors a long time, a couple of years to get used to investing in a world where money isn't free

insights.claim: After the launch of the consumer AI agents Muse and Instinct, which can find and cancel subscriptions, Goldman Sachs' 'consumer inertia' basket sold off programmatically, dragging down names like New York Times (down 7.2% in a couple of days) that Michael Batnick says face no real disruption risk because of their loyal audience.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Quant basket selling hits good and bad names alike. Pick out the non-disrupted members (NYT versus, say, Planet Fitness) for mean reversion.
insights.quote: It's in a basket of stocks. And so it is programmatically happening. There's nobody thinking it's the quant shops.

insights.claim: Charles Schwab reliably sells off whenever a disruptive AI product appears. When Hazel launched, Schwab, LPL and Raymond James fell about 10%, yet when Vanguard bought Altruist, a real competitive threat, Schwab fell only about 40 basis points.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Josh Brown suggests a reflexive counter-trade: keep a list of stocks (Schwab, Adobe) that dump on every AI headline and buy the overreaction.
insights.quote: Anytime there's a disruptive AI product on the tape like that's the poster ch like let's go beat the out of Schwab.

insights.claim: Josh Brown and Jonathan Boyar say multi-manager pod shops such as Millennium and Point72, which now take the bulk of hedge fund flows, give portfolio managers very short leashes (a drawdown of about 5% in a month draws risk-manager scrutiny), forcing de-risking that amplifies losers and creates entry points for three-to-ten-year investors.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Outsized drops with no news in crowded names often reflect forced pod de-grossing, a structural edge for patient capital.
insights.quote: selling begets selling

insights.claim: Jonathan Boyar says Booking Holdings (Booking.com, Priceline, Kayak) is wrongly sold as an AI-agent victim: ChatGPT launched instant checkout in September 2025 and backed off by March, Google and TripAdvisor failed to replicate Booking's global inventory, and small boutique hotels (some without websites), loyalty perks and heavy EU travel regulation mean agents like Muse will route through Booking.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Boyar
insights.so_what: Boyar owns Booking and prefers it over Expedia. He sees AI agents as a distribution channel for its inventory, making AI-fear selloffs buying opportunities.
insights.quote: Muse isn't going to do all this stuff. They're going to use booking. This is a positive for booking

insights.claim: Booking fell from about $215 to $157 in September 2026 alone. The hosts warn the forward multiple (about 15x) can keep derating even if the fundamentals are right, while Jonathan Boyar cites lower oil, a resolution in Iran and fading AI fears as catalysts.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Travel names carry both AI-fear and oil and geopolitical sensitivity. An Iran ceasefire or lower oil could be the trigger for a rerating.
insights.quote: You could be right on the fundamentals and still wrong on the stock

insights.claim: Josh Brown argues that a single partnership announcement with OpenAI or Anthropic could end an AI-fear derating, as happened when Salesforce put Dario on stage at Dreamforce. Jonathan Boyar counters that companies should not sign premature exclusive deals because AI model leadership keeps shifting between ChatGPT and Claude.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Watch for AI-lab partnership announcements from derated incumbents as potential rerating catalysts (the Salesforce playbook).
insights.quote: I think one announcement with Open AI and and the D-rating is over.

insights.claim: Salesforce (CRM), which Jonathan Boyar was bullish on during the early-2026 'SaaS apocalypse' when the stock was hammered, rebounded after partnering with Anthropic, and Boyar says a similar setup is now forming in other AI-fear names.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: This is a precedent for buying software and platform incumbents during AI-disruption panics when the business is intact.
insights.quote: They have partnered with Anthropic rather than having their throat slit by it.

insights.claim: A host notes travel may be the number-two or number-three ad category on Google, so if Gemini-style agents replace travel searches, Google could lose meaningful ad revenue. The disruption risk may cut against Google as much as the online travel agencies.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Agentic search may cannibalize Google's own high-value travel ad inventory, a second-order risk for Alphabet.

insights.claim: Jonathan Boyar calls the AI-agent selloff in Airbnb, a stock he likes, 'nonsensical' because an agent like Muse cannot deal directly with every homeowner renting out a property. The stock gapped up about 10%, ran from $150 to $190, and is back to about $150.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Boyar
insights.so_what: Airbnb's hard-to-replicate supply is a moat against AI agents. Boyar treats the round trip back to $150 as a buying opportunity.

insights.claim: Uber's stock fell the day after CEO Dara Khosrowshahi reportedly bought about $10 million of shares and the CFO about $5 million, even with a corporate buyback running, robotaxi partnerships live in several cities and guidance unchanged since January. The host fears it heads toward 12 times earnings.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Heavy insider buying and buybacks are not moving the stock, which is a sentiment-driven mispricing if growth holds.
insights.quote: This feels like it's going to trade at 12 times earnings.

insights.claim: Jonathan Boyar says Uber cannot stay at its current valuation if it keeps growing 20-30% a year with free cash flow of roughly $10 billion expected in 2027. He would advise management to keep a cash cushion, buy back as much stock as possible and consider a tender offer.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Boyar
insights.so_what: The FCF yield on Uber looks high relative to its growth. A tender offer or larger buyback would be the catalyst to watch.
insights.quote: I think it's almost impossible if it's going to continue growing at 20 to 30% a year for the stock to stay the way it is.

insights.claim: Uber is making equity investments in autonomous-vehicle fleets and OEMs across Europe, the US and Asia to seed non-Waymo, non-Tesla robotaxi supply, a reversal from two years ago, and the market is giving it no credit for them.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Uber is positioning as the aggregator for third-party AV fleets. Any visible return on these stakes could rerate the stock.

insights.claim: The hosts point to Meta as proof that for broken stocks (as opposed to broken businesses) the turn can come faster than a technical setup allows. Uber, like Meta, has intact earnings estimates, so waiting for confirmation risks buying 20% higher.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Separate broken stocks from broken businesses. For the former, a starter position beats waiting for the chart.
insights.quote: these were not broken businesses

insights.claim: Broadridge, an ADP spin-off that handles about 80% of proxy votes with 63% recurring revenue, has fallen from about $280 to $160 (about 25% down this year) in its second-worst drawdown since the GFC. The bear case is that tokenized stocks remove the need for proxy services, which Jonathan Boyar dismisses.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Boyar
insights.so_what: Boyar sees a near-monopoly regulatory toll booth derated on AI and token fears. The catalyst is the market realizing the business is not disrupted, and AI may even lift margins internally.
insights.quote: one of the bare cases is these tokens uh that where you can trade stocks, they're not going to have to do proxies

insights.claim: Jonathan Boyar says Broadridge, with an enterprise value of about $20 billion, could plausibly be acquired and cross-sells boring niche services such as filing shareholder class-action claims for money managers, unlike Fiserv, whose back-office story blew up under a former CEO.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Boyar
insights.so_what: M&A is optional upside for Broadridge. Boyar considers the company well run, which distinguishes it from the Fiserv blowup.

insights.claim: Pool Corp, the largest US pool-supply distributor, has fallen from over $500 to about $167 and trades near 15 times earnings, the multiple it had in the financial crisis and after 9/11, versus 55 times at the COVID peak, when revenue grew about 27% annualized and pulled demand forward.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Boyar
insights.so_what: The multiple has reset to crisis levels while maintenance revenue from a much larger installed base of pools is recurring, a classic reset from overvalued compounder to value.
insights.quote: sold for 55 times earnings

insights.claim: US new pool construction has averaged about 60,000 a year for two years, the lowest in over a decade, and is interest-rate sensitive (HELOC-financed), but most of Pool Corp's revenue comes from maintenance chemicals and equipment for the installed base that must be serviced every summer.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: The market prices Pool Corp on new construction while the maintenance base is annuity-like. Rate cuts could be an upside catalyst.

insights.claim: Jonathan Boyar first recommended Pool Corp at $20 in 2009 and re-recommended it in summer 2026 at about 17-18 times earnings. He cites a board with distribution backgrounds, extremely low leverage and no controlling shareholder as making it a plausible private-equity or Berkshire-type target, even though Berkshire Hathaway sold its stake after Todd Combs left.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Boyar
insights.so_what: A takeover floor adds to the case, though Boyar would rather compound Pool Corp long term than be bought out.
insights.quote: it is a cheap cheap stock now

insights.claim: Restaurant Brands International (QSR: Burger King, Tim Hortons, Popeyes, Firehouse Subs) is holding up better than peers because executive chair Patrick Doyle, whose tenure at Domino's saw about a 20x gain, is halfway through a Burger King North America turnaround that Jonathan Boyar says McDonald's is only starting, despite 20-25% beef inflation.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Boyar
insights.so_what: QSR is a relative-strength turnaround within a weak restaurant group. Improving franchisee economics and same-store sales are the metrics to track.
insights.quote: they're basically halfway through the recovery that McDonald's is just starting

insights.claim: Jonathan Boyar expects 3G Capital to stay invested in Restaurant Brands long term, collecting a 3-4% yield while it looks for more restaurant acquisitions. He says a new take-private is harder at an enterprise value of about $45 billion, while noting the original Burger King take-private may be the best percentage private-equity deal ever.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Boyar
insights.so_what: A committed anchor owner plus a dividend supports the downside. M&A upside is less likely at the current size.

insights.claim: Jonathan Boyar calls Comcast cheap at 5-6 times EBITDA as the Roberts family appears ready to exit and the company splits into NBCUniversal and broadband, but says the broadband business faces tough competition from fixed wireless and Starlink, making Comcast less interesting than his other names.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Boyar
insights.so_what: Comcast is a deep-value, sum-of-the-parts split trade rather than a quality compounder. Broadband subscriber losses are the key risk.
insights.quote: at five or six times Ebida, it's pretty cheap

insights.claim: Jonathan Boyar says he has learned to avoid businesses that consumers hate, citing StubHub (which he wrote up but did not buy), because of its convoluted story and ownership structure. Michael Batnick describes being charged about $9,000 after StubHub let one ticket sell seven times, which he calls a profit center for the company.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Boyar
insights.so_what: Consumer hostility is a red flag for durability and regulatory risk. It is a screen worth applying to marketplace businesses.
insights.quote: one of the things I think I've learned uh is to not buy businesses or or look at businesses that are hated by consumers

insights.claim: MGM Resorts fell about 10% after Barry Diller (via IAC) pulled his takeover bid, leaving it near $33 a share at about 16 times earnings. Jonathan Boyar expects Diller to come back.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Boyar
insights.so_what: A renewed bid is a near-term catalyst on top of a reasonable standalone multiple.
insights.quote: I think he's going to come back.

insights.claim: Jonathan Boyar says MGM will open the only casino in Japan around 2031 with a Japanese partner and at least a four-to-five-year head start. He expects revenue close to MGM's Vegas business, which analysts are not modeling.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Boyar
insights.so_what: The Japan integrated resort is unmodeled long-dated upside. Watch for sell-side estimate revisions as opening approaches.
insights.quote: in 2031 they're going to have the only casino in all of Japan

insights.claim: Jonathan Boyar views the weakness in Las Vegas visits by Canadians as temporary, expects BetMGM to be fine as prediction markets such as Kalshi get regulated, and flags MGM's China exposure as a reason to size the position carefully.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Boyar
insights.so_what: Size gaming positions for China risk while treating the Canadian-tourism drag and prediction-market competition as transitory.
insights.quote: People aren't going to Vegas from Canada because the Canadians hate the Americans. That's going to change.

insights.claim: Sports-betting and casino stocks are broadly out of favor: Flutter is at an all-time low as DraftKings, Caesars, BetMGM and now Robinhood compete intensely, and Las Vegas Sands has fallen from $70 in December to $38.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Competitive intensity, including from Robinhood, is compressing online-betting economics, so be selective within gaming.
insights.quote: Flutter's at an alltime low today.

insights.claim: A host relays an unverified claim that Hard Rock pays Florida about $500 million for exclusive gambling-app rights, with the Seminole tribe involved, which is why DraftKings is absent from Florida.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: State exclusivity deals can shut national sportsbooks out of large markets, a structural limit on TAM.

insights.claim: VICI Properties, the S&P 500 REIT that owns 103 assets including Caesars Palace, MGM Grand and the Venetian, has fallen from about $33 last summer to $23. The host says casino operators sold their real estate to VICI under activist pressure and used the cash for buybacks at the top.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Even the 'safe' yield landlord of the Strip is being derated along with casino sentiment, so the Vegas slowdown is showing up in REIT pricing.
insights.quote: the REIT looks even worse than the casinos
